site.title: Mushrooms of the Delaware Water Gap and Sourlands
site.tagline: A living field gallery — grouped by genus, mapped by GPS.
site.disclaimer: This site is for education and appreciation only. It is not a foraging guide. Never eat a wild mushroom unless an expert has confirmed the identification.

groups.edibility: Many toxic or deadly — treat all as poisonous unless expertly identified
groups.summary: A diverse genus of mycorrhizal gilled mushrooms. Includes white buttons (possibly destroying angels), yellow patches, warty Lepidella types, and pale striate grisettes. Free white gills and a volva at the stem base are classic clues.
groups.uses: Not recommended for foraging. A few species are edible only for experts; many are deadly (amatoxins). Photograph, study, do not taste.
groups.habitat: Forest floor under hardwoods after rain; ectomycorrhizal.
groups.tree_associates: Oaks, beech, birch, and mixed hardwoods of the Sourlands and Water Gap.
groups.field_marks: Free white gills; often a ring and/or volva; warts or patches on many caps; white spore print.

groups.edibility: Variable by species — never eat without confident ID
groups.summary: Fleshy mushrooms with pores under the cap instead of gills. Includes brown boletes, orange-capped Leccinum-types, two-colored boletes (Baorangia bicolor), and pale boletes of oak woods.
groups.uses: Some are choice edibles when correctly identified and cooked; others are bitter or cause GI upset. Avoid red-pored unknowns.
groups.habitat: Soil among leaf litter; mycorrhizal. Peak after summer rains.
groups.tree_associates: Oaks especially; also beech, pine, aspen depending on genus.
groups.field_marks: Pores (sponge underside); thick stems; fleshy caps.

photos.caption: Two-colored bolete — red-orange cracked cap, yellow pores

id_detail.edibility: Edible when correctly identified and well cooked (caution)
id_detail.summary: Red-orange cracked cap with bright yellow pore surface and reddish stem in oak litter. Matches the eastern two-colored bolete.
id_detail.uses: Considered a good edible by many when ID is certain and cooked thoroughly; some get mild GI upset. Not for beginners.
id_detail.habitat: Oak woods on the forest floor after summer rains; mycorrhizal.
id_detail.tree_associates: Strongly associated with oak (Quercus).
id_detail.field_marks: Red to orange cap (often cracked); yellow pores; stem red over yellow; no true gills.

photos.caption: Orange-tan bolete — cap top among oak litter

id_detail.edibility: Variable — do not eat without species ID
id_detail.summary: Smooth orange-tan to cinnamon bolete cap with a thick pale stem in oak leaf litter. Pore surface not fully visible; genus-level ID pending closer underside details.
id_detail.uses: Some orange-brown boletes are edible when correctly identified; others are bitter. Confirm pores, bruising, and species before any use.
id_detail.habitat: Soil among hardwood leaf litter; mycorrhizal.
id_detail.tree_associates: Oaks and mixed hardwoods of the Sourlands.
id_detail.field_marks: Orange-tan fleshy cap; thick stem; pores under cap (not gills).

groups.edibility: Variable — many acrid; do not eat without species ID
groups.summary: Colorful brittle-fleshed woodland mushrooms. Red-capped species are common on Sourland oak floors after rain.
groups.uses: A few mild species edible when cooked; many peppery. Ecologically important mycorrhizal partners.
groups.field_marks: Brittle chalky flesh; colorful caps; no veil on most species.
groups.region_notes: Very common in Sourland oak woods.

id_detail.habitat: Forest floor under hardwoods; mycorrhizal.
id_detail.tree_associates: Oaks, beech, pine, mixed stands.
id_detail.field_marks: Brittle chalky flesh; red/pink cap; white gills; no veil on most species.

groups.habitat: Dead and dying hardwood logs and stumps.
groups.tree_associates: Oaks and other hardwoods; beefsteak often on oak.
groups.field_marks: Pores or smooth underside; shelves or crusts on wood.

id_detail.edibility: Sometimes listed as edible but often ignored; not recommended without expert ID
id_detail.summary: Small to medium gilled mushroom with a hygrophanous orange-brown, often depressed and shiny-wet cap center, pale margin, and whitish stem in oak litter. Common “oak-loving collybia” complex (Gymnopus dryophilus and allies).
id_detail.uses: Historically eaten by some when carefully identified; many look-alikes exist. Better treated as a study species than food.
id_detail.habitat: Leaf litter under hardwoods, especially oak; saprobic on litter.
id_detail.tree_associates: Oaks and mixed deciduous litter of eastern forests.
id_detail.field_marks: Hygrophanous tan to orange-brown cap; often umbonate or depressed when wet; white to pale gills; thin pale stem; on litter not wood shelves.
